length: Term 1 Weeks 4–7 · 9 lessons and the CAT (3 a week)
description: Students learn that matter is anything with mass that takes up space, then build and test the particle model: particles that are always moving, held by attractions, further apart in liquids and gases. They use the model to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases, including melting and boiling points, viscosity, diffusion, expansion and density, and meet its limits. Three experiments (mass and space, a cooling curve, density by displacement) build the measuring and graphing skills the CAT draws on.
notes: **Lesson rows follow the 2027 scope and sequence** (T1 W4–W7). The Lesson Booklet has 15 lessons for this content, so some rows teach two or three booklet lessons; the booklet lessons not set in class are listed as homework or optional.
Booklet Lessons 16–27 (pure substances, solutions, separation) are now the **Separation Techniques** unit in Term 2.

**Audit key terms** — melting point (Lesson 5), density (Lessons 8–9), viscosity (Lesson 1) and particle motion (Lesson 4) — are now in the learning intentions. **Viscosity is not yet in the booklet or decks.** {{PH:viscosity activity sheet}}
**Above level:** elements, compounds and formulas (VC2S8U07) appear only in Part D.

print.text: Whole Lesson Booklet (190 pp., Lessons 1–27 — this unit is Lessons 1–15, pp. 3–124)

achievement.text: Use the particle model to explain the properties and behaviour of solids, liquids and gases — including changes of state, melting and boiling points, viscosity, diffusion, expansion and density — in terms of the arrangement, motion and attraction of particles.

Make predictions; plan safe, fair investigations and select equipment that measures mass, volume, temperature and time precisely; organise data in tables and line graphs; analyse patterns and identify sources of error.
Explain how new evidence can lead to changes in scientific models (what a scientific model is; the limits of the particle model).

descriptors.text: The particle and kinetic theories describe the arrangement and motion of particles in a substance, including the attraction between them, and explain properties such as melting and boiling points, density, compressibility, gas pressure, diffusion and expansion
Scientific knowledge, including models and theories, can change in light of new evidence
Science inquiry — questioning and predicting (I01); planning and conducting (I02–I03); processing, modelling and analysing (I04–I05)
Levels 7–8, above level in this unit — atomic theory, elements and compounds, symbols and formulas (Part D only)

prepare: Lesson 1’s opening quiz checks primary-school ideas about solids, liquids and gases.
Every later deck opens with a review quiz on the lessons before.
review: Part C of each booklet lesson checked in class; exit questions; the three experiment write-ups.
diff: Every lesson opens with a short reading; every worked example (I do) is followed by a We do.
Particle-diagram templates with the container drawn; a word bank; pre-drawn graph axes; a red worked first row in every write-in table; a density formula triangle.
extension: Part D of each booklet lesson — plasma, non-Newtonian fluids, why the model is a theory, density columns.
Booklet Lesson 12 (gas pressure) and the parts of Lessons 5–6 not set in class.

lessons.title: States of matter
li: Know that matter is anything with mass that takes up space.
Describe solids, liquids and gases by shape, volume, flow and compressibility.
Compare how easily liquids flow — viscosity — and classify tricky materials.
sc: I can sort materials into solid, liquid or gas and give evidence from their properties.
I can rank liquids by viscosity.
guided: Booklet Lesson 1 — [pp. 3–12](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=3): A reading *The Stuff Everything Is Made Of*; B Worked Examples 1.1–1.3 with We do; C Tasks 1.1–1.9; D Extensions
Viscosity: race honey, oil and water down a tile {{PH:viscosity activity sheet}}
PhET *States of Matter: Basics*, run from the board
review: Opening quiz — what students already know
Exit question: classify a material and give two pieces of evidence

lessons.title: What is a scientific model?
li: Explain what a scientific model is and why scientists use one.
Infer what is inside a sealed box from evidence.
Say what makes one model better than another.
sc: I can use evidence to build a model, and say one strength and one limitation of it.
explicit: [Lesson 2 · What is a Scientific Model?](deck2.html) slides
guided: Mystery-box activity: shake, tilt and listen, then draw what is inside

lessons.title: Lab: dry ice demo and Experiment 1 — matter has mass and takes up space
li: Show that gases have mass and take up space.
sc: I can describe an experiment showing that air has mass, and read a balance and a measuring cylinder.
explicit: [Lesson 3 · Experiment 1](deck3.html) slides — using a balance, reading a measuring cylinder
Dry ice demonstration (teacher only): sublimation, and the gas inflating a balloon

prac.name: Matter has mass and takes up space — a flat and a pumped-up ball on a balance; the upturned cup in a tub of water
prac.si: Use a balance and a measuring cylinder to take precise readings, and record them in a table (VC2S8I03).
prac.su: Explain, with evidence, that gases are matter: they have mass and take up space (VC2S8U05).
prac.risk: {{PH:RiskAssess link — Experiment 1 and dry ice demo}}

lessons.title: The particle model
li: Describe the arrangement, spacing, motion and attraction of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Explain that particles are always moving, and move faster when heated (particle motion).
Use particle diagrams to explain each state’s properties.
sc: I can draw a particle diagram of each state and use it to explain why liquids flow and gases compress.
explicit: [Lesson 5 · Particles Are Always Moving](deck5.html) slides (Brownian motion)
guided: Booklet Lesson 4 — [pp. 32–40](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=32): students act out the three states
Booklet Lesson 5 — [pp. 41–48](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=41): particle motion — Part C as homework
Booklet Lesson 6 *The Limits of the Model* — [pp. 49–56](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=49) with [its slides](deck6.html): optional, or the misconception card sort as a starter
review: Particle diagrams checked against the three rules
Exit question: why can a gas be squashed but a solid cannot?

lessons.title: Changes of state
li: Name every change of state, including sublimation, and explain each with particles and energy.
Explain melting point and boiling point, and use them to identify a substance.
Tell evaporation from boiling.
sc: I can explain a change of state using particles and energy, and state what happens at the melting point.
guided: Booklet Lesson 8 *Boiling, Evaporation and Condensation* — [pp. 65–71](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=65): Part C as homework
PhET *States of Matter* — Phase Changes screen
review: Exit question: why does sweat cool you?

lessons.title: Lab: observing changes of state — Experiment 2, a cooling curve
li: Explain the flat section of a cooling curve with particles and energy.
sc: I can draw a cooling curve and explain why the temperature stays steady while it freezes.

prac.name: A cooling curve — temperature of a cooling substance over time
prac.si: Record temperature at regular time intervals; draw a line graph and describe the pattern (VC2S8I03, VC2S8I04, VC2S8I05).
prac.su: Identify the freezing point from the graph and explain why temperature stays constant during a change of state (VC2S8U05).
prac.sheet: Booklet Lesson 9 — [pp. 72–80](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=72): results table, graph grid and analysis

lessons.title: Expansion, contraction and diffusion
li: Explain diffusion with moving particles, and predict how temperature changes its speed.
Explain expansion and contraction — particles move further apart; they do not grow.
Give engineering examples of designing for expansion.
sc: I can explain why food colouring spreads faster in hot water, and why bridges have expansion joints.
guided: Booklet Lesson 10 *Diffusion* — [pp. 81–88](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=81): food colouring in hot and cold water (predict, then observe)

lessons.title: Density
li: Explain density with particle spacing and mass.
Calculate density with \(D = m \div V\) and correct units.
Predict floating and sinking from density.
sc: I can calculate density and use it to predict whether an object floats in water.
guided: Booklet Lesson 14 *Calculating Density* — [pp. 110–116](booklet/Particle_Model_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7.pdf#page=110): Part C as homework
Density column with honey, oil and water (demo)
review: Density calculations in Part C checked

lessons.title: Lab: volume displacement — Experiment 3, density by displacement
li: Identify a material from its density.
sc: I can find the volume of an irregular object by displacement and calculate its density.

prac.name: Density by displacement — mass and volume of five objects
prac.si: Measure volume by displacement and mass on a balance; process the data to calculate density (VC2S8I03, VC2S8I04).
prac.su: Use density to identify a material and predict whether it floats (VC2S8U05).

review: Density results checked before the CAT

lessons.title: CAT — Particle Model
li: Use the particle model to explain properties and changes of state, and process experimental data.
sc: I can explain properties with particles and calculate density under test conditions.
